sense: something that must be met first

evidence: Cic. Arch. 25: sed eā condiciōne, nē quid posteā scrīberet
terms.comment: “On condition that” is eā condiciōne ut (or nē) with the subjunctive; to turn down the terms, condiciōnem respuere (Caes. BG 1.42, Lewis & Short). The spelling conditiō is a manuscript error that took the word for a derivative of condō (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: sēnsus plērumque cōmicus: Plaut., Ter.; also Cato
evidence: Ter. Eun. 102: hāc lēge tibi meam adstringō fidem
terms.comment: Hāc lēge, eā lēge ut, on these terms; in this sense mostly before Cicero (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Accius in Cic. Off. 1.97: ōderint, dum metuant
Cic. Brut. 285: dummodo sit polīta (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The negative is dum nē, dummodo nē.

phrases.latin: jubēre eī praemium tribuī, sed eā condiciōne, nē quid posteā scrīberet
phrases.english: (we saw Sulla) order a reward to be given him, but on condition that he write nothing more

phrases.latin: vērum heus tū, hāc lēge tibi meam adstringō fidem: quae vēra audīvī taceō et contineō optumē
phrases.english: but listen, I give you my word on this condition: what I hear that’s true, I keep to myself and hold in perfectly
the drones refuse; the bees accept the terms
